For the marketing team

RackTrack, feature by feature.

Everything the product does, in plain English, with pictures of the real screens. Each part below says what it is, why a customer would care, and the one shot in it worth filming. Nothing here needs any technical knowledge to read.

For planning the customer film Parts 23 Screens shown 50 Put together 7 August 2026
Start here

The whole thing in one paragraph

Somebody points a phone at a rack of equipment and takes one photograph. Seconds later they have a list of everything in it, a map of every socket and cable, a check on whether the software is up to date, a priced list of what to buy, and a note pointing at everywhere the company's own records disagree with what the camera just saw.

Everything below is a version of that sentence. If a scene in the film cannot be traced back to it, it probably belongs in a follow up conversation instead.

Who is watching

Four people see this film, and they want four different things

The order matters less than making sure nobody sits through three minutes without hearing their own problem named.

The person running operations

Wants to know their team stops copying labels onto a clipboard. Sold by the photograph and what comes back.

The network engineer

Is looking for the catch. Sold by depth, the sockets, the cables, the live network view. Give them one dense screen and they relax.

The person who buys things

Wants to stop over ordering and stop buying the wrong part. Sold in ten seconds by the shopping list.

The person who signs off audits

Wants proof with a date on it. Sold by the records check and the diary of what changed.

Priorities

The three moments that sell it

If time or budget is short, protect these three and let everything else be a quick montage. Each one is a single continuous shot, and each is hard to answer with a slide.

  • The photograph coming back

    One picture goes in, and the rack comes back with everything in it named and placed. Do not cut while it is thinking.

    See section: What comes back

  • Pulling back from the rack

    One rack turning in three dimensions, then the camera pulls back until the whole row fills the screen.

    See section: The rack drawn out

  • The disagreement

    The company records on one side, the photograph on the other, and the line that does not match flagged between them.

    See section: Checking against your records
The product

Everything it does

In the order a customer meets it. Two of these have no picture yet, and they are marked.

01

Getting in

Two ways to join a team, and both take under a minute.

Someone starting a new company account fills in a short form and gets a code by email to prove the address is theirs. Everyone after that joins from an invitation link, which already knows who they are and which site they belong to. People can also sign in with a Google, Apple or Facebook account.

Why it matters

A whole field team gets set up by forwarding a link. There is no training day and no rollout project.

What to film

The invitation link opening straight into a half filled form. Three seconds is plenty.

02

The opening screen

The first thing anyone sees, and the sentence we already lead with.

The app opens on one claim, "Every rack. Every unit. Precisely documented", set beside a photograph of a real aisle. Everything else in the product is a way of backing that sentence up.

Why it matters

It is the product saying what it is in six words. The film can borrow the line as it stands.

What to film

A good opening or closing frame. The words are already on screen, so no caption is needed.

03

Taking the photo

Point a phone at a rack and take one picture. That is the whole job.

There are three ways to start. Take the picture there and then, use one already saved on the phone, or record a short video. While the person is lining up the shot the app tells them what to fix, such as come closer or hold still, and it will not let them take a picture it cannot read properly.

Why it matters

What used to take a trained engineer fifteen to twenty minutes with a clipboard now takes one photograph, and the person holding the phone does not need to be an expert.

What to film

The app coaching someone into a good shot, then the button unlocking. It is the product visibly looking after the person using it, and it makes what happens next feel earned.

04

A whole row at once

Walk the aisle with the camera running and get every rack back, one by one.

Instead of one rack, film a slow walk along a row. The app picks the best moment for each rack, reads them all, and keeps them together as one job. There is also a mode for capturing just two racks side by side, and one for a rack too tall to fit in a single picture.

Why it matters

The unit of work stops being one rack and becomes a whole aisle. This is the answer to "yes, but we have four hundred of them".

What to film

One continuous walking shot down a real aisle, phone up, then the whole row appearing on screen. This is the most cinematic thing the product does.

05

What comes back

The same photograph, with everything in it named and put in its place.

A few seconds after the picture goes in, it comes back with every piece of equipment outlined and labelled, shelf by shelf, from top to bottom. Tap anything to look closer, or tell the app it got something wrong and it takes the correction.

Why it matters

This is the moment that sells the product. Everything else in the app is built on this one result.

What to film

Hold on the picture as the outlines and labels draw themselves onto it. Do not cut while it is thinking. Let the wait play out, because the wait is what makes it believable.

06

Every socket on the switch

Which sockets are in use, which are free, and what kind they are.

The app asks the switch itself which of its sockets are busy and which are spare, and what type each spare one is. A simple bar shows how full the switch already is.

Why it matters

It answers the question the engineer is standing there asking, which is whether there is room to plug something in and whether their cable will actually fit.

What to film

The bar filling up. Small, but it is the shot that says this is live information, not a photograph.

07

Following a cable

Tap one end and see where the other end goes.

Pick any cable and the app shows what kind it is and what sits on the far end of it. There is also a mode where you pick two pieces of equipment and it draws the path between them.

Why it matters

This is the knowledge that lives in one senior engineer's head and leaves the building when they go on holiday. It is now written down automatically, every time somebody takes a picture.

What to film

A finger taps one socket and the cable lights up across the rack to its far end. It reads instantly, even with the sound off.

08

The rack drawn out

The rack rebuilt as a drawing you can turn around and look inside.

Two views of the same rack. A flat front on drawing, like the one an engineer would sketch on paper, and a three dimensional version you can spin, tilt and zoom, with the cables drawn in as coloured tubes. You can hide cables by type, or recolour everything by how full it is.

Why it matters

It makes a rack that nobody on the current team built readable in about five seconds.

What to film

Start close on the rack, spin it once, then pull the camera back until the whole row is in frame. This is the best looking thing we have. Build the film around it.

09

Checking against the live network

Not what the photograph showed, but what the network itself says right now.

Most of the app works from the picture. This part talks to the running network instead and lines up what was photographed against what is really switched on and connected at this moment.

Why it matters

This is the screen for the person in the room who has been waiting to find the catch. Give them one dense, technical screen and they relax.

What to film

Opening one piece of equipment to reveal its full live list. Deliberately dense. Five seconds is enough.

10

Everything about one switch

One card per switch, telling you who it is and what it can do.

The app reads the make and model off the front of the switch, then does the looking up for you. One card holds three things: the manufacturer's own published details, whether the software on it is current, and which plug in parts fit it.

Why it matters

An engineer can check a switch on sight, without logging into it and without having seen it before.

What to film

Flick between the three tabs on one card. It shows how much is under the surface in about four seconds.

11

Looking up any device

Type a make and a model, get the manufacturer's own numbers back.

Normally somebody opens a browser, guesses the manufacturer's website, digs through product pages, finds the right document and scrolls to the table. The app goes and reads it for you, and gives you a link back to the page it came from so anyone can check.

Why it matters

It settles an argument in seconds, using the manufacturer's own page rather than somebody's memory.

What to film

Two boxes, one button, a full table of answers. Keep it to five seconds. It supports the story, it is not the story.

12

Is the software up to date

A green light, an amber light, and an honest grey one.

Give it the make, the model and the version running today. The app goes to the manufacturer's own site, finds the newest version they publish, and answers in a colour you can read in a second. If it genuinely cannot confirm, it says so rather than guessing.

Why it matters

Deciding what to upgrade first stops being a spreadsheet job. Anything badly out of date rises to the top of the list on its own.

What to film

The amber answer landing. One frame, one colour, and it needs no explaining.

13

What changed, and when

A running diary of every socket on a switch.

For any switch the app is watching, it checks in on a schedule and writes down anything that actually changed, and at what time. Something came on at two in the afternoon. Something got faster at quarter past nine. Somebody moved a cable at twenty to eleven.

Why it matters

The annoying problems that nobody can pin down, a connection that keeps dropping, a cable somebody moved and did not write down, stop being detective work.

What to film

Scrolling the diary of one socket across a few months and stopping on the day it changed.

14

Checking against your records

Your records say one thing. The camera saw another. The app raises it, with the picture attached.

This works both ways. It can write a freshly photographed rack into the company records system, though never quietly, it asks for sign off first. And it can go the other way, comparing what the records expect against what the camera actually saw, and flagging anything that disagrees.

Why it matters

It does not replace the records system they already have. It is the thing that finally makes that system true. Their system stays exactly where it is, it just stops being wrong.

What to film

The record on one side, the photograph on the other, and the line that disagrees marked between them. Set up a real disagreement before filming, because a check that finds nothing is a dead scene.

No screenshot yet. This screen still needs capturing before the film is planned around it.
15

The report, and sending it

The whole visit as one document, sent straight to the people who need it.

Every scan can be opened as a full report and saved as a file, or sent from inside the app straight into Slack, Teams or an email, with a note attached. The app remembers who you last sent to.

Why it matters

This is the thing that actually leaves the app. Everything else produces knowledge, and this is the screen where that knowledge lands in somebody else's inbox as proof.

What to film

The report opens, one tap, and it is in a Slack channel. Strong candidate for the closing shot, because it is the moment a week of work becomes an attachment.

No screenshot yet. This screen still needs capturing before the film is planned around it.
16

Buying the right part

Empty sockets on a switch turn into a shopping list with a price on it.

The small plug in parts that go into a switch are fussy. They have to match the socket, the speed and the brand, and you need enough of them. Starting from a switch the app already recognised, it works out what fits, shows a first choice and some alternatives with real prices and pictures, and counts how many are needed to fill every empty socket.

Why it matters

They stop buying things they already own, and they stop ordering the wrong part, because the list came from what the camera saw rather than a spreadsheet somebody last updated months ago.

What to film

Empty sockets turning into a priced list with the quantity filling itself in. The line for the screen is simple: from photograph to purchase order, with nothing typed in between.

17

Buying and selling gear

The switch that just came out of a rack, listed for sale in two taps.

A place inside the app to move hardware. List spare kit for sale, put up a wanted advert, or search an outside marketplace with the details already filled in. A listing can be created straight from something the camera identified, so a buyer can see it came from real equipment rather than a typed description.

Why it matters

Equipment coming out of service turns back into money, and the advert carries proof of what it actually is.

What to film

The sell button on a scan result filling in the advert by itself. It closes the loop the film opened with, because the same photograph is still doing work several screens later.

18

Orders and delivery

It is not a noticeboard. Things get bought, and things get posted.

A buyer goes through a proper checkout with a delivery address and an order summary. The seller gets a screen where they mark something as sent and add a tracking number, and their own dashboard showing everything they have listed and how it is doing.

Why it matters

The difference between saying you have a marketplace and having one is whether money and a parcel actually move. This is the proof they do.

What to film

The tracking number going in on the seller side. Two seconds, and it settles the question.

19

Alerts and outside marketplaces

Say what you are hunting for, and let the app watch for it.

Save a search and the app tells you when something matching turns up, keeping an inbox of matches. If a part is not listed inside, it can search outside marketplaces with the details already filled in, and those accounts can be connected so their listings show up alongside.

Why it matters

The hard to find part finds them, instead of somebody remembering to check every week.

What to film

An alert arriving against a saved search. Worth five seconds in a montage, no more.

20

Connecting your own systems

Where the app is told how to reach the systems the customer already runs.

The app can talk to the record keeping and network systems a company already has. This screen is where those are added. Passwords go in and are never shown again, and although many can be saved, only one is in use at a time, so the whole app follows when you switch.

Why it matters

It is the answer to "we already have a system for this". Good, keep it. The app feeds it.

What to film

Two seconds at most, just enough to show the familiar logos. Never film a password being typed.

21

Teams and sites

Companies, the sites inside them, and the people at each one.

One console with two levels. The person running the platform sees every customer and can set one up, approve one, or switch one off. Somebody running a single company sees only their own, with their sites, their people and the invitations going out.

Why it matters

It is the proof that one customer can never see another customer's racks, shown rather than promised.

What to film

A brief pan across the list. The names in these pictures have been blurred, and they must stay blurred or be replaced with made up ones before anything is filmed.

22

Your account and everything you have scanned

Every rack you have ever photographed, newest first, one tap from opening again.

Who you are signed in as at the top, and underneath, everything you have photographed, with a small picture of each, what was found in it and how long ago. Tap any one and the whole thing opens again exactly as it was. It follows the account, not the phone.

Why it matters

Documentation stops being something they have to produce and becomes something they already have.

What to film

Scrolling a long list of real scans. The more there are, the better it looks, so fill this account up before filming.

23

Ask DOT

A built in assistant that answers questions about the app in plain English.

A help screen with an assistant that answers questions about how the app works, alongside the most common questions already laid out, and a guided walk through for somebody using it for the first time.

Why it matters

It is the answer to "who on my team has time to learn this".

What to film

Optional. If the film is running long, this is the first thing to cut.

Keep these out

Four screens that stay in the building

These are real parts of the product, but each one shows something a customer should not see.

The accuracy tool

An internal screen that asks a technician to confirm or correct the things the app was least sure about. It is one of the cleverest parts of the product, and it is built entirely around the app being wrong. That is a fine conversation in a room where somebody can ask a follow up question, and a bad one in a film that gets forwarded without us.

The platform owner's dashboard

Shows activity across every customer at once, which means one customer's information sitting next to another's. It should never be in front of a client, on film or otherwise.

The activity log

Worth saying out loud that everything is recorded. Not worth showing, because it is a wall of rows and it looks like nothing.

The engineering screen

An internal screen for checking the system is healthy. It exists in the app and it should never appear on camera.

Before filming

Six things worth sorting out first

All of them are far cheaper to get right on the day than to fix afterwards.

  1. There is no augmented reality feature, so do not plan one.

    An old project document still describes one. It is not in the product. If anybody has read that and is planning a scene around it, drop it now rather than in the edit.

  2. Real names and email addresses appear on some screens.

    They are blurred in this document. Before filming, replace them with made up ones. The same goes for any equipment names, addresses and serial numbers, because a picture of a company's equipment is a map of it.

  3. Nothing on screen should let a viewer reach the app.

    No web address, no company name in the corner, no sign in screen with a real address in it. This film goes to people who are not getting the product yet.

  4. Fill the account up before filming.

    Several screens in this document look empty because the test account has nothing in it. A long list of past scans and a busy marketplace make the product look used. Empty screens make it look abandoned.

  5. Do not cut while the app is thinking.

    When the picture goes in and the finished rack comes back, let it run in one piece. A magician does not cut away in the middle of a trick, and a cut there reads as something being hidden.

  6. The room matters as much as the app.

    The film lives or dies on the footage of a real aisle, the lighting, the depth, the long view down the corridor. A great screen recording in a bad room still looks like a school project.

If a screen here looks empty, or you want a picture of something that is missing, ask the product team and we will capture it properly. Nothing in this document should end up in the film without being checked first.
